qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture fifteen. High-performance computing. Many small workers, wired together, run one big job.
On Priya’s laptop, the storm model takes three days. The regatta is on Saturday.
On a laptop, the storm model takes 3 days.
Three things make a system fast. Processing does the sums, communication moves data, and I O reads and writes.
Three things make a system fast: processing, communication, I/O.
A supercomputer is one huge machine, or many computers on a network. Kestrel, the university cluster, is the second kind.
One giant machine, or many computers on a network.
A cluster holds nodes, each node holds processors, and each processor holds cores.
A cluster has nodes; nodes hold processors; processors hold cores.
Four nodes, times two processors, times eight cores. Sixty-four cores at once.
4 × 2 × 8 = 64 cores working at once.
One sum or product on decimal numbers is one floating-point operation.
One sum on decimal numbers is a floating-point operation.
FLOPS counts how many of them a machine does in one second.
FLOPS: how many of them a machine does per second.
Giga, tera, peta, exa. Each rung is a thousand times the one below.
Giga, tera, peta, exa: each rung is 1000 times the last.
A server processor reaches one to two teraFLOPS. A data-centre GPU such as the H one hundred goes past a thousand.
A server CPU: 1 to 2 TFLOPS. A data-centre GPU: over 1000.
Kestrel’s nodes are joined by a local area network, a LAN.
Nodes are joined by a LAN, a local-area network.
At every step, each node swaps the weather at its border with its neighbours.
Each step, every node swaps border weather with its neighbours.
On a slow network, the fast cores finish their sums and sit waiting for data.
A slow network leaves fast cores waiting for data.
Moore’s law says the transistors on a chip double about every two years.
Moore's law: transistors on a chip double about every two years.
One, two, four, eight, sixteen. After ten years, thirty-two times as many.
1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Ten years: 32 times as many.
Now chips are hitting their limits and falling behind that line.
Now chips are hitting limits and falling behind.
So extra speed comes from more cores and more nodes.
So new speed comes from more cores and more nodes.
Take a small job. Ten sums must run in order, and a hundred more can be shared out.
10 sums must run in order. 100 more can be shared.
On one processor, that is a hundred and ten sums in a row.
On 1 processor: 110 sums in a row.
On ten processors, the hundred split ten ways. The ten in order still go one by one.
On 10 processors the 100 split ten ways. The 10 do not.
The job takes the time of twenty sums. A speedup of five and a half, not ten.
Time of 20 sums: a speedup of 5.5, not 10.
This is Amdahl’s law. The sequential part sets the limit.
The sequential part sets the limit.
p is the share of the time that can be shared out. s is how much faster that part gets.
p: the share of time that can be shared. s: its speedup.
With ninety per cent shareable, eight processors give four point seven, and sixty-four give eight point eight.
90% shareable: 8 processors give 4.7×, 64 give 8.8×.
The ten per cent in order never shrinks, so the speedup can never beat ten.
It can never beat 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10×.
With only half shareable, even thirty-two processors stay below two.
50% shareable: even 32 processors stay below 2×.
Owning a supercomputer means paying for staff, support, power and cooling. Electricity alone can reach eight hundred million dollars a year.
Owning it costs admins, support, power and cooling.
So a resource manager shares it out. It decides which hardware each job gets, and who runs when.
A resource manager allocates hardware and schedules the work.
It also starts the work on many nodes, and watches it while it runs.
It starts the work on many nodes and monitors it.
Jobs wait in a queue that sets the order. When one finishes, the next one runs.
Each job waits in a queue that sets the order.
Kestrel’s resource manager is Slurm. It is open source, modular, extensible and scalable.
Slurm: Kestrel's resource manager and scheduler.
Slurm splits the nodes into partitions. The cpu partition has six, the gpu partition two, and each is a queue.
Partitions: cpu has 6 nodes, gpu has 2. Each is a queue.
The highest priority job goes first and takes four nodes. The next one takes the last two.
The high-priority job takes 4 nodes, the next takes 2.
No nodes are left, so the third job waits.
No nodes left: the third job waits.
Priya submits job four zero two one with sbatch. Three nodes are busy with an older job, so it waits.
sbatch submits job 4021. Nodes are busy, so it waits.
squeue shows it pending. When the older job finishes, it gets n one to n four.
squeue shows it pending, PD. Then it gets n1 to n4.
srun launches a job step of four tasks, one on each node.
srun launches a job step: 4 tasks, one per node.
Afterwards, sacct shows the record. The job completed in about five hours and twelve minutes.
sacct shows the record: completed in 5 h 12 min.
A cluster’s power is nodes times processors times cores, counted in FLOPS.
Amdahl’s law says the part that must run in order caps the speedup.
Slurm shares the machine through partitions and priority, with four commands from submit to record.
